title: Modify Cloud Resource Hierarchy
summary: Cloud providers organise tenants, accounts, subscriptions and resource groups in a hierarchy so that policy and billing can be applied to whole groups at once. This technique describes adversaries editing that hierarchy rather than the workloads inside it. In Azure, an actor holding a Global Administrator role may create new subscriptions or move a pay-as-you-go subscription into a tenant they control, which lets them consume the victim's compute while the activity is logged only on the attacker side. In AWS, an account with the right permissions may call LeaveOrganization to detach itself from its organisation, dropping the service control policies and guardrails inherited from it, or call CreateAccount to add a fresh account inside the organisation that inherits the same payment method but none of the tuned detections. Defenders should treat control-plane events on organisation, management group, subscription and account objects as high-signal: they are rare, attributable to named principals, and usually generated by change management. A subscription or account that changes parent, or a new account that appears without a matching business record, is the clearest differentiator from legitimate administration.

beginner.definition: This is when an attacker changes the structure of a cloud account instead of the servers inside it. Cloud platforms let you group accounts and subscriptions into folders, so rules can be applied to many at once. An attacker with high permissions can move, add or remove those groups. The goal is to escape the rules and monitoring that protect the original part of the cloud.
beginner.whyItMatters: Rules that protect a cloud account often come from the group it belongs to. If the account leaves that group, the rules stop applying. The attacker can then use the victim's computers and storage, often without the victim seeing logs. This can also make the victim pay the bill. Because so few people ever change these settings, a change is a strong warning sign that should be checked quickly.
howItWorks: The attacker first steals the keys or login of an account with high cloud permissions. In Azure that could be a global administrator, and in AWS an organisation owner.
They look at how the cloud is arranged, listing which accounts and subscriptions sit under which groups.
In Azure, they may create a brand new subscription and place their own resources inside it.
They may also move an existing subscription into a tenant they control. Your own records then stop showing that activity.
In AWS, they may detach an account from its organisation, which removes inherited guardrail rules. They may instead add a new account with no tuned alerts.
Afterwards, they deploy their own workloads or keep quiet access, and less of it appears in your logs.
beginner.example: Think of a large office building with floors that share a master key policy. Every floor gets the same access rules and the same camera coverage because the floors belong to the building. Now imagine someone edits the building directory so one floor is officially listed as a separate outside building. The cameras and door rules for that floor no longer apply. As far as the system knows, it is no longer part of your building. The floor is still attached, and you still pay its electricity, but the guard sees nothing.
takeaways: The cloud structure itself is a target, not just the servers inside it.
Inherited rules only apply while the account stays in the group, so watch for moves.
A subscription or account changing parent is rare and worth an alert.

objectives: Describe how cloud resource hierarchies pass rules down to the accounts inside them.
Explain how creating or moving a subscription or account can remove inherited protections.
Identify the control plane log sources that record organisation and subscription changes.
Distinguish a routine planned hierarchy change from an attacker escaping guardrails.
Explain why activity in a moved subscription may be missing from the victim's logs.
